label: ANOVA Tables and Degrees of Freedom — unseen mastery test

items.stem: In a CRD, the total number of observations is N and there are a treatments. The treatment degrees of freedom are:
items.explanation: There are a fitted treatment means subject to one grand-mean constraint, leaving a−1 independent treatment contrasts.

items.stem: The correction factor used in the computational ANOVA formulas is:
items.explanation: G is the grand total and N is the number of observations. Subtracting G²/N centres the raw sum of squares around the grand mean.

items.stem: A CRD has 5 treatments and 25 observations. What is the error df?
items.explanation: Error df is N−a=25−5=20. There are 25 observations and five fitted treatment means, leaving 20 residual degrees of freedom.
items.check: df check: treatment 4 + error 20 = total 24 = N−1. The requested quantity is error df, 20.

items.stem: The treatment test in an ANOVA table uses:
items.explanation: The F statistic compares mean squares, which put the sources on a variance scale.

items.stem: A significant omnibus treatment F establishes that:
options: At least one treatment mean differs
The treatment effect is practically important
items.explanation: The null is equality of all treatment means. Rejection indicates not all means are equal; it does not identify the pair.

items.stem: For a complete RBD with a treatments and b blocks, block df are:
items.explanation: There are b block effects with one constraint, leaving b−1 df.

items.stem: In a CRD, a=4 treatments and N=20. The total df are:
items.explanation: Total df=N−1=19; treatment plus error df are 3+16=19.
items.check: Treatment df=3, error df=16 and total df=19; their identity is 3+16=19.

items.stem: In a complete RBD with a=5 treatments and b=4 blocks, error df are:
items.explanation: For a complete randomised block design, error df=(a−1)(b−1)=4×3=12. The treatment and block contrasts account for the remaining model degrees of freedom.
items.check: For a complete RBD, error df=(a−1)(b−1)=4×3=12. There are four independent treatment contrasts and three independent block contrasts.

items.stem: A CRD has treatment SS=60 and error SS=40 with 4 treatments and N=20. Its treatment F statistic is:
items.explanation: Treatment df=3 and error df=16. MS treatment=20, MS error=2.5, so F=8.
items.check: MS treatment=60/3=20 and MS error=40/16=2.5; the ratio is 20/2.5=8.

items.stem: An RBD has treatment SS=80, residual SS=20, 5 treatments and 4 blocks. Treatment F is:
items.explanation: Treatment df=4; error df=12. MS values are 20 and 5/3, hence F=12.
items.check: MS treatment=80/4=20 and MS error=20/12=5/3; F=20÷(5/3)=12.

items.stem: Consider the following statements about a balanced completely randomised design.
items.explanation: A, B and C are true. Treatment df=a−1; error df=N−a; total df=N−1. Statement D is false because treatment F is MS treatment divided by MS error, not SS treatment divided by SS error.
statements: The treatment F statistic is SS treatment divided by SS error.

A.why: There are a treatment means subject to one constraint, so a−1 independent treatment contrasts remain.

B.why: Subtracting the a fitted treatment means from N observations leaves N−a residual degrees of freedom.

C.why: The grand mean is estimated, leaving N−1 total degrees of freedom.

D.why: The F ratio compares mean squares, not raw sums of squares.

items.stem: In a complete RBD, the reason for including a block row is to:
options: create additional replications of every treatment
remove predictable nuisance variation from residual error
items.explanation: Blocks capture a known nuisance source such as field position. Treatments are still randomised within blocks, and each block contains all treatments.

items.stem: A complete RBD has 4 treatments and 3 blocks. Total df are:
items.explanation: N=ab=12, so total df=11. The component df are 3+2+6=11.
items.check: With 4 treatments and 3 blocks, N=12 and total df=N−1=11; component df are 3+2+6=11.

items.stem: Consider a complete randomised block design with a treatments and b blocks.
items.explanation: A, B and C hold. Treatment df=a−1; block df=b−1; error df=(a−1)(b−1). Statement D is false: one observation in each cell leaves no within-cell replication to separate interaction from residual error.
statements: RBD treatment degrees of freedom are a−1.
RBD block degrees of freedom are b−1.
RBD error degrees of freedom are (a−1)(b−1).
With one observation per cell, treatment-by-block interaction is separately estimable.

C.why: The remaining cell variation has (a−1)(b−1) degrees of freedom.

D.why: There is no within-cell replication, so interaction cannot be separated from residual error.

items.stem: In the CRD example with treatment totals 30, 42 and 26, each based on 4 observations, N=12 and G=98. Treatment SS equals:
items.explanation: Treatment SS=(30²+42²+26²)/4−98²/12=32.6667. The total SS is 33.6667 and error SS is 1.
items.check: Use treatment totals: (30²+42²+26²)/4−98²/12=32.6667. The target is treatment SS, not total SS.

items.stem: A significant treatment F is obtained in a complete RBD. Which follow-up statement is defensible?
options: The treatment with largest sample mean is necessarily best
The block effect must also be significant
At least one treatment mean differs; use planned contrasts or a post-hoc method to locate differences
items.explanation: The omnibus null tests equality of all treatment means. Its rejection does not identify which means differ or rank practical performance without additional comparisons and context.

items.stem: In a complete RBD with 6 treatments and 5 blocks, treatment SS=125 and error SS=25. Calculate the treatment F statistic.
items.explanation: Treatment df=5 and error df=20. MS treatment=25; MS error=1.25; F=20.
items.check: Treatment df=5 and error df=20. MS treatment=125/5=25; MS error=25/20=1.25; F=25/1.25=20.

items.stem: Consider the model and interpretation of a complete RBD with one observation in each treatment-block cell.
items.explanation: A, B and D are true. The additive model contains treatment and block effects; standard ANOVA assumes independent errors with common variance; blocks do not replace randomisation. Statement C is false because one observation per cell cannot identify interaction separately from residual error.
statements: The additive RBD model includes a treatment effect and a block effect.
The ordinary RBD ANOVA assumes independent errors with a common variance.
With one observation per cell, the treatment-by-block interaction can be tested separately from error.
Blocks are nuisance groups and do not replace treatment randomisation.

B.why: Independence and common variance are standard ANOVA error assumptions; normality supplies exact finite-sample F inference.

C.why: There is no within-cell replication, so interaction cannot be tested separately.

D.why: All treatments are still randomised to experimental units within each block.

items.stem: A CRD has 3 treatments and N=15. Treatment SS=72 and error SS=18. Its treatment F statistic is:
items.explanation: Treatment df=2 and error df=12. MS treatment=72/2=36, MS error=18/12=1.5, so F=36/1.5=24.
items.check: F uses mean squares, not raw SS: 36/1.5=24. Degrees of freedom check: 2+12=14=N−1.

items.stem: A balanced CRD and a complete RBD have the same number of observations. Why can the RBD treatment F be larger?
options: The RBD makes all treatment means equal
The RBD increases the number of observations
The RBD changes the treatment df to N−1
The RBD removes a block source from residual error when the block effect is real
items.explanation: The RBD can reduce residual SS by accounting for systematic block differences. With a comparable treatment SS and a real block effect, residual MS may fall, increasing treatment F.
